meta.titre: Perfect Competition: features, price-taking firms and why profit returns to normal
meta.sous_theme: Features of a perfect market and the position of the firm

sections.contenu_markdown: On a market day in a town in the Grassfields, dozens of sellers display almost identical bags of maize or heaps of tomatoes, and hundreds of buyers walk round comparing. A seller who asks far more than the going price sees buyers walk away to the neighbouring stall. This situation is close to what economists call perfect competition. It is a model, because no real market meets every condition, but GCE papers regularly ask you to name its features and to explain why a single firm has no power over the price.

items: A market is any arrangement that brings buyers and sellers of a good together.
Total revenue equals the price per unit multiplied by the quantity sold.
Profit equals total revenue minus total cost.

sections.titre: Features of perfect competition and the firm's position
sections.contenu_markdown:
### Features of a perfect market

| Feature | Meaning |
|---|---|
| Many buyers and many sellers | Each is so small that none can affect the price by buying or selling more or less. |
| Homogeneous product | The goods sold by all firms are identical, so buyers do not prefer one seller. |
| Free entry and exit | New firms can enter the market, and unsuccessful ones leave, without barriers. |
| Perfect knowledge | Buyers and sellers know the prices and conditions in the market. |
| Perfect mobility of factors | Workers and other resources can move easily to where they earn most. |

### The firm is a price-taker
The market price is set by the demand and supply of the whole industry. Each firm is a **price-taker**: it accepts the market price and can sell any quantity it likes at that price. If it charged more, buyers would go to other sellers; there is no reason to charge less. The price per unit is the same as the revenue per unit, so average revenue and marginal revenue both equal the price, and total revenue rises in proportion to output.

### Profit in the short run and in the long run
In the short run a firm may earn abnormal (supernormal) profit, normal profit or a loss, depending on the price. If firms earn abnormal profit, new firms are attracted in, industry supply rises and the market price falls. This continues until firms earn only **normal profit**, the minimum reward needed to keep the entrepreneur in business and counted as part of costs. If firms make losses, some leave, supply falls and the price rises.

Perfect competition is rarely met in full; markets for basic farm produce come closest to it.

variantes.quand_utiliser: When the question asks for the features or characteristics of a perfect market
variantes.contenu_markdown: Name each feature and add a short explanation, such as: many sellers, so no single seller can influence the price.

variantes.quand_utiliser: When a firm's output and total cost are fixed and the price changes
variantes.contenu_markdown: Total revenue is the price times output. Compare with total cost: more means abnormal profit, equal means normal profit only, less means a loss.

variantes.quand_utiliser: When the question asks what happens after firms enter or leave the market
variantes.contenu_markdown: Entry raises industry supply and lowers the price; exit does the opposite. The movement stops when firms earn normal profit only.

sections.enonce_markdown:
A tomato farmer in a perfectly competitive market takes the market price of 500 FCFA per kg. The table gives her total cost at different outputs.

| Output (kg) | Total cost (FCFA) |
|---|---|
| 10 | 4,000 |
| 20 | 6,500 |
| 30 | 9,000 |
| 40 | 12,500 |
| 50 | 22,000 |

(a) Calculate total revenue at each output.
(b) Calculate profit at each output.
(c) Which output gives the greatest profit?
(d) Why can she not raise her price to 550 FCFA and still sell the same output?

etapes.action: Calculate total revenue at each output.
etapes.justification: Total revenue is the market price times the quantity sold.

etapes.action: Subtract total cost from total revenue.
etapes.justification: Profit = total revenue minus total cost.
The profit-seeking firm chooses the output with the highest profit.
etapes.resultat_markdown: The greatest profit is **7,500 FCFA** at an output of **40 kg**. At 50 kg the extra cost of the last 10 kg (9,500 FCFA) is greater than the extra revenue (5,000 FCFA).

etapes.justification: Buyers can find the identical tomatoes elsewhere at the market price.
etapes.resultat_markdown: At 550 FCFA buyers would go to the other sellers, so she would sell nothing. She takes 500 FCFA.

sections.conclusion_markdown: (a) 5,000; 10,000; 15,000; 20,000 and 25,000 FCFA. (b) 1,000; 3,500; 6,000; 7,500 and 3,000 FCFA. (c) 40 kg, with a profit of 7,500 FCFA. (d) The product is homogeneous and there are many sellers, so a firm that raises its price loses all its customers.

items.erreur_markdown: "In perfect competition each firm decides its own price."
items.pourquoi_faux: A firm with a tiny share of the market has no power over the price.
items.correction_markdown: Each firm is a price-taker; the price is set by the demand and supply of the whole industry.

items.erreur_markdown: "Goods in a perfect market are similar, but each seller has a brand name."
items.pourquoi_faux: Brands and differences between products mean the goods are not identical. This is typical of imperfect markets.
items.correction_markdown: Homogeneous means identical: buyers see no difference between one seller's goods and another's.

items.erreur_markdown: "Firms in perfect competition earn large profits for ever."
items.pourquoi_faux: With free entry, abnormal profit attracts new firms. Supply rises and the price falls.
items.correction_markdown: In the long run firms earn only normal profit.

items.erreur_markdown: "A perfect market has one large seller who controls the supply."
items.pourquoi_faux: A single large seller is a monopoly. Perfect competition has many small sellers.
items.correction_markdown: There are many buyers and many sellers, and none can influence the price.

items.erreur_markdown: "A firm in perfect competition can sell more only by lowering its price."
items.pourquoi_faux: A firm facing the market price can sell as much as it can produce at that price.
items.correction_markdown: It sells any quantity at the market price. Lowering the price would only reduce its revenue per unit.

items.enonce_markdown:
(a) State two features of a perfect market.
(b) A firm in a perfectly competitive market sells 15 kg of beans at the market price of 800 FCFA per kg. Calculate its total revenue and state its average revenue per kg.
items.solution_markdown:
(a) Any two of: **many buyers and sellers**, **homogeneous product**, **free entry and exit**, **perfect knowledge**, **perfect mobility of factors**.
(b) Total revenue $= 15 \times 800 =$ **12,000 FCFA**. Average revenue per kg is the price, **800 FCFA**.

items.enonce_markdown:
A farmer produces 60 kg of rice, with a total cost of 18,000 FCFA (including normal profit). Find the total revenue and the result for each market price, and say what kind of profit or loss it is.
(a) 350 FCFA per kg
(b) 300 FCFA per kg
(c) 250 FCFA per kg
items.solution_markdown:
(a) $60 \times 350 = 21\,000$ FCFA. Profit $= 21\,000 - 18\,000 =$ **3,000 FCFA**, which is abnormal profit.
(b) $60 \times 300 = 18\,000$ FCFA. Revenue equals cost, so the farmer earns **normal profit only** (break-even).
(c) $60 \times 250 = 15\,000$ FCFA. Result $= 15\,000 - 18\,000 =$ **a loss of 3,000 FCFA**.

items.enonce_markdown:
Many maize farmers sell in a perfect market at 400 FCFA per kg. Each farmer sells 50 kg at a total cost of 15,000 FCFA. After some time many new farmers enter and the market price falls to 300 FCFA per kg.
(a) Calculate a farmer's profit at 400 FCFA per kg.
(b) Explain why new farmers entered.
(c) Calculate a farmer's profit when the price is 300 FCFA per kg and say why entry stops.
(d) Explain why one farmer could not stop the fall in price by cutting his own output.
items.solution_markdown:
(a) Total revenue $= 50 \times 400 = 20\,000$ FCFA. Profit $= 20\,000 - 15\,000 =$ **5,000 FCFA**.
(b) Abnormal profit attracted new farmers, since entry into the market is free.
(c) Total revenue $= 50 \times 300 = 15\,000$ FCFA. Profit $= 15\,000 - 15\,000 =$ **0**, so only normal profit is earned (normal profit is already counted in costs). With no abnormal profit nothing more attracts entry, so it stops.
(d) Each farmer supplies only a tiny part of the market output, so cutting his own output hardly changes the industry supply and the price stays the same.

items_markdown: Perfect competition has many buyers and sellers, a homogeneous product, free entry and exit, perfect knowledge and mobile factors.
Each firm is a price-taker: the price is set by industry demand and supply, and the firm sells any quantity at that price.
For a price-taking firm average revenue and marginal revenue equal the price.
Abnormal profit attracts new firms, supply rises, price falls, and in the long run firms earn normal profit only.
Perfect competition is a model; markets for basic farm produce come closest to it.
